title: Agile maturity assessments and cumulative flow diagrams
blurb: Explain what agile maturity assessments measure and when they start, and read a cumulative flow diagram to find bottlenecks and work in progress.
question: Which progress technique shows the number of tasks in each workflow state over time, helping a team spot a bottleneck?

teach.body: The progress practice in PRINCE2 Agile names three techniques: agile maturity assessments, cumulative flow diagrams and burn charts. Burn charts track what is delivered. The other two answer different questions. Maturity assessments ask how agile the people and teams really are, and whether that is improving. A cumulative flow diagram asks how smoothly work is flowing through a team's workflow, and where it is getting stuck.

Agile maturity is first assessed in starting up a project or in initiating a project. The assessment rests on three key metrics for agility: psychological safety, agile maturity and agile sustainability. This sets a baseline; the same metrics are then checked regularly, which is one way the progress practice monitors progress. In directing a project, the agile enablement workshop runs regular Agilometer assessments so that agile maturity and the risks of agile working are reviewed regularly.

teach.body: A cumulative flow diagram (CFD) is a visual picture of how many tasks sit in each stage of the workflow over time. It helps identify bottlenecks and assess overall progress. It is mainly a team-level tool, for example on a team's Kanban board, and is unlikely to be used at project level. It sits naturally alongside flow metrics such as lead time and work-in-progress limits.

teach.h: A CFD with a testing bottleneck
teach.caption: The gap between 'In test' and 'Done' keeps widening: work enters testing faster than it leaves. That band is the bottleneck.

teach.body: Each band between two lines is one workflow state. The band's height on any day is the number of items in that state, so a band that keeps getting taller means work is arriving faster than it leaves: a likely bottleneck. Bands running parallel show a steady flow. A Done line that goes flat means nothing is being finished. The usual response is to limit work in progress and have the team help clear the blocked state.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 12.4.2; Kanban background

teach.body: Pennine's claims portal project assessed agile maturity in initiation; psychological safety scored low, so agile coach Grace Whitfield worked with the board on it, and later assessments showed it rising. Mid-stage, team coach Arjun Shah shows the claims team its CFD: the 'In review' band has doubled in height over two weeks while Done is barely rising. The team agrees a work-in-progress limit for review and swarms on the queue before starting new stories.

teach.text: Do not mix up the charts. A CUMULATIVE FLOW DIAGRAM shows tasks in each workflow state (bottlenecks, mostly team level). A BURN CHART shows work done and left. A CUMULATIVE RISK BURN-DOWN shows total risk exposure across iterations (risk practice). And maturity is assessed with agile maturity assessments, not with OKRs.

summary: You can now say when agile maturity is first assessed and which three key metrics it uses, and how maturity is reviewed through the project. You can also read a cumulative flow diagram to spot a bottleneck and tell it apart from burn charts and the cumulative risk burn-down.

A.q: When is agile maturity first assessed in a PRINCE2 Agile project?
options: In starting up or initiating a project
In the first team retrospective workshop
A.why: 12.4.1: agile maturity is initially assessed during starting up a project or initiating a project.

whyNot.0: Stage boundaries come later; the first assessment is at the start of the project.
whyNot.2: Closure uses maturity trends in the lessons report; it is not the first assessment.
whyNot.3: Retrospectives reflect on an iteration; maturity is first assessed in starting up or initiating.

A.q: Which are the key metrics for agility used in agile maturity assessments?
options: Velocity, lead time, cycle time and throughput
Scope tolerance, cost tolerance and time tolerance
Psychological safety, agile maturity and agile sustainability
Objectives, key results and benefits realized so far
A.why: 12.4.1 and 2.7.6: the assessment is based on psychological safety, agile maturity and agile sustainability.

whyNot.0: Velocity, lead time and cycle time measure delivery flow, not agility.
whyNot.1: Tolerances are set on performance aspects; they are not metrics for agility.
whyNot.3: OKRs and benefits track goals and value, not agile maturity.

A.q: What does a cumulative flow diagram show?
options: Tasks in each workflow state over time
Skills and gaps across the team
A.why: 12.4.2: a CFD is a visual representation of tasks in the different stages of the workflow over time.

whyNot.1: Total risk exposure across iterations is a cumulative risk burn-down.
whyNot.2: Completed work against a deadline is a burn-up chart.
whyNot.3: Skills and gaps are shown in a team skill matrix.

B.q: At which level is a cumulative flow diagram MOST likely to be used?
B.why: A CFD tracks tasks through a team's workflow and is unlikely to be used at project level (12.4.2).

whyNot.0: The board uses the project dashboard, not task-level flow charts.
whyNot.1: The business layer sets project tolerances; it does not track task flow.
whyNot.2: A CFD is unlikely to be used at project level.

B.q: On a team's CFD, the 'In test' band grows steadily taller each week while the Done line rises slowly. What does this MOST likely show?
options: The team is ahead of its iteration plan
Scope has been removed from the backlog
B.why: A CFD helps identify bottlenecks (12.4.2): a band that keeps widening means work enters that state faster than it leaves.

whyNot.0: A slowly rising Done line suggests the opposite of being ahead.
whyNot.2: Removing scope would lower the top line, not widen the testing band.
whyNot.3: Psychological safety is measured in agile maturity assessments, not a CFD.

B.q: In which workshop are regular Agilometer assessments run so that agile maturity and agile risks are reviewed regularly?
B.why: The agile enablement workshop, for the board, agile coaches and business representatives in directing a project, holds regular Agilometer assessments (13.3.3).

whyNot.0: The progress review workshop reviews project dashboard metrics, risks and a product demo.
whyNot.1: The team retrospective covers the good, the bad, the learning and team building.
whyNot.3: The kickoff covers team intro, values, skill matrix, delegation matrix and dashboards.

C.q:
Which two statements about progress techniques in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?
1. A cumulative flow diagram helps identify bottlenecks.
2. OKRs are the main way to assess agile maturity.
3. Agile maturity assessments include psychological safety.
4. A cumulative flow diagram tracks total risk exposure.
C.why: A CFD helps identify bottlenecks (1), and agile maturity assessments are based on psychological safety, agile maturity and agile sustainability (3) (12.4.1, 12.4.2).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: OKRs are not used to assess agile maturity.
whyNot.2: Both are wrong: OKRs do not assess maturity, and risk exposure is a cumulative risk burn-down.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: total risk exposure is tracked with a cumulative risk burn-down.

C.q: A board wants to know whether agile ways of working are taking hold across the project's teams, and how this is changing over time. What is the BEST source?
options: The OKRs set at release planning
C.why: Agile maturity assessments, baselined early and repeated, show agility over time; their trends appear on the project dashboard (12.4.1, 12.3.2.1).

whyNot.1: Burn-downs show work remaining in an iteration, not agility.
whyNot.2: CFDs show flow and bottlenecks in a team's workflow, not agile maturity.
whyNot.3: OKRs align teams on goals; they are not used to assess agile maturity.

C.q: A team's CFD shows its 'In review' band widening for two weeks. Which response BEST fits the purpose of the chart?
options: Raise an exception report to the project board
Re-run the agile maturity assessment for the team
Limit work in progress and help clear the review queue
Replace the CFD with a project-level burn-up chart
C.why: A CFD exists to reveal bottlenecks (12.4.2); the team acts on the bottleneck, for example by limiting work in progress and swarming on the queue.

whyNot.0: A team-level bottleneck is not, by itself, a forecast breach of stage tolerance.
whyNot.1: A maturity assessment measures agility, not a queue in the workflow.
whyNot.3: A burn-up shows completed work at project level; it would hide the bottleneck.

reteach.title: A health check and a motorway camera
reteach.question: Which tells you how fit you are, and which tells you where traffic is stuck?

blocks.body: A yearly health check tells you how fit you are, and whether that is improving: that is an agile maturity assessment, checking psychological safety, agile maturity and agile sustainability. A traffic camera above a motorway shows where cars are piling up between junctions: that is a cumulative flow diagram, showing which workflow state is clogging. Different gauges, different questions.

blocks.text: A widening band on a CFD is a traffic jam in that state, not a sign of progress.

test.q: Which is a technique of the progress practice in PRINCE2 Agile?
test.why: 12.4 lists agile maturity assessments, cumulative flow diagrams and burn charts as progress techniques.

whyNot.0: The Agilometer is a risk practice tool for assessing the risks of agile working.
whyNot.2: Delegation poker belongs to the organization practice.
whyNot.3: Magic estimation is a plans practice estimation technique.

explain.body: Agile maturity is first assessed in starting up or initiating, then checked again with the same metrics to show the trend (12.4.1, 12.2).

test.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. Agile maturity assessments are based on psychological safety, agile maturity and agile [?].
test.why: The three key metrics for agility are psychological safety, agile maturity and agile sustainability (2.7.6, 12.4.1).

whyNot.0: Velocity is a delivery metric, not one of the key metrics for agility.
whyNot.1: Governance matters in PRINCE2 Agile but is not one of the three key metrics.
whyNot.3: Estimation is a planning activity, not a key metric for agility.

explain.body: Tasks in each workflow state over time; helps identify bottlenecks and assess overall progress; mostly a team-level tool (12.4.2).

test.q: What does a cumulative flow diagram MAINLY help a team identify?
options: The date of its next release
test.why: 12.4.2: a CFD helps identify bottlenecks and assess overall progress.

whyNot.1: Total risk exposure is shown by a cumulative risk burn-down.
whyNot.2: Skill gaps are shown by a team skill matrix.
whyNot.3: Release dates are planned on the release map and forecast with burn-ups.

explain.body: Band height = items in that state. A band that keeps widening = a likely bottleneck. Parallel bands = steady flow. Flat Done line = nothing finishing.

test.q: On a CFD, all the bands run roughly parallel with a steadily rising Done line. What does this suggest?
options: A steady, stable flow of work
test.why: Parallel bands mean work enters and leaves each state at a similar rate, and a rising Done line means items keep finishing: a stable flow.

whyNot.0: A bottleneck shows as a band that keeps widening.
whyNot.1: Work stopping would show as a flat Done line.
whyNot.2: Shrinking scope would show the top line falling, not parallel bands.
